title: Eucratides and the Civil War of Kings

title_i18n.en: Eucratides and the Civil War of Kings

subtitle: Megas in the Mountains: How Eucratides Split the Greek East
era: Bactrian and Indo-Greek dynastic wars, c. 171-145 BCE
region: Bactria, Paropamisadae, Kabul valley and the Hindu Kush
moral: Civil war can break what conquest built.

sources.citation: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 41.6, trans. J.C. Yardley (1994)
sources.note: Only extended narrative for Eucratides' wars and death.

sources.citation: Eucratides I coinage, including the famous gold 20-stater in the Bibliotheque nationale de France
sources.note: Primary evidence for his title Megas and exceptional royal display.

sources.citation: Frank Holt, Thundering Zeus (1999); Bopearachchi, Monnaies greco-bactriennes et indo-grecques (1991)

panels.shot: low-angle dramatic wide of a stormy mountain pass with armies on both sides of the Hindu Kush

dialogue.text: In the high winds of Bactria, Eucratides Megas rose against his own kings—and broke the Indo-Greek world in two.

panels.shot: wide aerial over the Oxus valley

dialogue.text: A century after Alexander, Bactria was a rich hinge of the world—Greek cities on Iranian soil, guarding the passes to India.

panels.shot: slow push-in on a stylized timeline frieze of kings and coins

dialogue.text: Seleucid governors became Bactrian kings. Euthydemus held the Oxus; Demetrius carried Greek banners over the Hindu Kush into India.

panels.shot: intimate mid-shot inside a palace hall

dialogue.text: In this world of frontier kings, Eucratides first appears not as conqueror, but as a name on coins—Eucratides, later styled Megas, the Great.

panels.shot: close-up on Eucratides’ face lit by lamplight

dialogue.text: The record is silent on his youth. Coins show a resolute man, perhaps of noble blood, rising amid palace intrigues in Bactra.

panels.shot: dramatic interior wide of a dim council chamber

dialogue.text: Ancient Justin tells of a usurpation. Eucratides seized the Bactrian throne from those who ruled in Demetrius’ name.

panels.shot: low-angle royal proclamation scene

dialogue.speaker: eucratides_i
dialogue.text: From this day, Bactria has its own king.

panels.shot: macro shot of a coin being struck

dialogue.text: His first proclamations were of metal. Silver pieces bore his portrait and titles, spreading his claim along caravan roads.

panels.shot: epic battle wide in a rocky plain below snow peaks

dialogue.text: Justin speaks of Eucratides at war with Demetrius, ‘king of the Indians’—a civil war of Greeks on both sides of the mountains.

panels.shot: tense close-up on Eucratides in battle

dialogue.text: Our source tells of terrible odds, of Eucratides holding out with a handful against a far larger enemy. The details are lost; the struggle is not.

panels.shot: wide shot of a defensive night camp under siege

dialogue.speaker: eucratides_i
dialogue.text: We are Bactria. This earth is our wall.

panels.shot: dynamic overhead shot of battle turning

dialogue.text: In Justin’s compressed tale, Eucratides survives, his enemies beaten back. The exact fields are unnamed; the outcome is clear—Bactria holds.

panels.shot: interior of a mint with monumental feel

dialogue.text: With victory came display. In a bold stroke, Eucratides ordered a coin unlike any other of his world.

panels.shot: close-up on the massive gold stater in a hand

dialogue.text: This huge gold piece—twenty staters—bore his helmeted likeness and the title Megas. Modern scholars still marvel at its size and ambition.

panels.shot: montage wide of the coin traveling along trade routes

dialogue.text: Carried by caravans, his coins spoke for him in far markets—from Bactra’s walls to Gandharan bazars and beyond.

panels.shot: map-table overhead shot

dialogue.text: Yet his triumph had a price. By seizing Bactria, Eucratides split the old Euthydemid realm from the Indo-Greek domains to the east.

panels.shot: split-screen style wide of two thrones and two mountain ranges

dialogue.text: The Hindu Kush became not a frontier of empires, but a fault line within a Hellenistic house—a Bactrian kingdom here, Indo-Greek kings there.

panels.shot: somber palace interior, Eucratides older and pensive

dialogue.text: Justin ends with a dark stroke: Eucratides murdered by his own son, his body dragged beneath a chariot and left unburied.

panels.shot: shadowy, suggestive scene in a courtyard

dialogue.text: No other source confirms this grim picture. What it preserves is a memory of dynastic hatred, of a house tearing itself apart.

panels.shot: map wide of Central Asia with waves encroaching

dialogue.text: As rival Greek kings struggled, new forces gathered—nomad confederations and Parthian rulers, watching a fragmented frontier.

panels.shot: quiet museum-like close-up of Eucratides coins under glass

dialogue.text: Today, Eucratides Megas lives in metal: portraits, titles, and a giant gold coin, witness to a king whose civil war remade the map from Bactria to India.
